The commercial bank shall ensure adherence to the provisions of Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and Rules made thereunder [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications on this matter issued by the RBI based on advice from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India [S1].

A commercial bank shall review its risk assessment at least annually [S1]. The Board or a committee of the Board to which it has delegated power shall determine the periodicity of the risk assessment exercise, in alignment with the outcome of the risk assessment exercise [S1].

The bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e-documents thereof or Form No. 60 [S1]. Before temporarily ceasing operations, the bank must give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard [S1].

The 'at par' cheque facility offered by commercial banks to co-operative banks shall be monitored and such arrangements must be reviewed to assess risks including credit risk and reputational risk [S1]. The bank retains the right to verify the records maintained by the customer cooperative banks/societies for compliance with extant instructions on KYC and AML under such arrangements [S1].

Any remittance of funds by way of demand draft, mail/telegraphic transfer/NEFT/IMPS or any other mode and issue of travellers’ cheques for a value of ₹50,000 and above shall be effected by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques and not against cash payment [S1].

A commercial bank shall consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time, and publicly available information, for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations [S1].
The bank shall not collect account payee cheques for any person other than the payee constituent [S1].

The bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government [S2].

The disclosures required under the chapter on Financial Statements are intended only to supplement and not to replace disclosure requirements under other laws, regulations, or accounting and financial reporting standards [S3]. NOT FOUND

Yes, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP to carry out CDD in case of new customer onboarding for individual customers and Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers [S1]. This is listed under point (1) of paragraph 26 [S1].

If there is no change in KYC information for an LE customer, the bank must obtain a self-declaration via registered email, ATMs, digital channels, a letter from an authorized official, or a board resolution, while ensuring Beneficial Ownership (BO) information is accurate and up-to-date [S1]. If there is a change in KYC information, the bank must undertake the KYC process equivalent to onboarding a new LE customer [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure it has KYC documents meeting current CDD standards, and if validity has expired during periodic updation, it must undertake the new customer onboarding KYC process, and verify PAN details if available [S1].

A commercial bank shall obtain any two of the listed documents or their equivalent e-documents as proof of business/activity for a proprietary firm [S1]. This requirement is also stated for Payments Banks [S2].
The bank shall not require CDD of all the members of an SHG while opening the savings bank account of the SHG [S1]. The CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].

A commercial bank shall categorise customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on its assessment and risk perception [S1]. The bank may lay down broad principles for the risk-categorisation of customers [S1].

The bank shall put in place a system of periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts, with such periodicity being at least once in every six months [S1]. For periodic updation of KYC, the frequency depends on the risk category: at least once in every two years for high-risk customers, once in every eight years for medium risk customers, and once in every 10 years for low-risk customers from the date of opening or last KYC updation [S4].
A bank must disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers so that customers can make an informed judgment about their product choice [S1].

All aspects concerning the renewal of overdue term deposits must be laid down in a transparent, non-discretionary, and non-discriminatory policy, and the terms and conditions, including interest rates, must be notified to the customer upon deposit acceptance [S1]. Advance instructions for deposit disposal on maturity should be obtained in the application form, or the bank must send advance intimation of the impending due date [S2].

The existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Responsible Business Conduct as applicable to Commercial Banks stand repealed with the issue of these Directions [S4]. The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, must be available in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language [S1].

A bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are in place and appropriate security measures are taken in each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold and/or silver collateral [S1]. Furthermore, the gold and/or silver collateral must only be handled in its branches and only by its employees [S1].

A bank shall be guided by Reserve Bank’s instructions on interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters as prescribed in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S1]. These Directions are called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S3].

A commercial bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with concentration of exporters to facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters [S1]. Additionally, a bank should open Export Counsel Offices to guide exporters, especially small ones and those engaged in non-traditional exports [S2].

The policy must cover the auction procedure, specifying the trigger event for the auction of eligible collateral and the timeline for serving an auction notice upon the borrower [S1]. It must also cover the mode of auction, the notice period allowed to the borrower(s) / legal heir(s) for loan settlement before auction, and the empanelment of auctioneers [S1].

A bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum in a BSBD account, with or without charges, provided it is done in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure to the customer [S1]. However, the bank shall not require the customer to maintain a minimum balance in the BSBD account while offering these additional facilities [S1]. The availment of these additional facilities is at the option of the customer [S1].

A bank shall undertake at least an annual review for accounts with no customer-induced transaction for more than a year [S1]. The bank must inform account/deposit holders in writing about no operation in the last one year [S1].

Warnings against placing deposits in dubious schemes can be displayed or distributed in bank branches in the official language of the state [S1]. The bank may also consider places like ATMs or Business Correspondent Points for wider visibility [S1].

Yes, the bank, as principal, is responsible for the actions of its agents [S2]. Therefore, it must ensure that its agents engaged for recovery of dues strictly adhere to the instructions while in the process of recovery [S2].

A bank shall have "Enquiry" or "May I Help You" counters either exclusively or combined with other duties, located near the entry point of the banking hall, at all branches excluding very small branches [S1]. The file/folder containing detailed information may be kept in the customer lobby of the branch or at the 'May I Help You' counter or at a place frequented by most customers [S2].
The prescribed post-shipment interest rate will cease from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account [S1].

The bank shall undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits [S1]. Additionally, a bank shall conduct public awareness and financial literacy campaigns regularly to educate the public about the activation of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits and the procedure to claim amounts [S2].

A bank must conduct regular audits of service providers, including subcontractors, regarding the outsourced service [S1]. These audits can be performed by the bank's internal or external auditors [S1]. The audits should assess the service provider's performance, risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations, with frequency determined by the nature and extent of risk [S3].

The selection of a group entity by a commercial bank shall be based on objective reasons similar to the selection of a third-party [S1]. The bank must also appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that the outsourcing arrangement may entail [S1].

The bank or NBFC shall be responsible for the actions of its service provider, including Direct Sales Agents (DSAs) / Direct Marketing Agents (DMAs) and recovery agents [S1, S2]. The bank or NBFC shall retain ultimate control of the outsourced activity [S1, S2].

A commercial bank shall ensure that the service provider, if not a group company, shall not be owned or controlled by any director, or key managerial personnel, or approver of the outsourcing arrangement of the bank, or their relatives [S1]. An exception to this requirement may be made with the approval of Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight and monitoring of such arrangements [S1].

It suffices if there is clear separation and isolation of data (bank, and its customer specific data and information) to ensure that only personnel authorized by the bank can access data belonging to them in a multi-tenant environment/architecture [S1].

Outsourcing arrangements entered into by a bank shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability of the customers to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws [S2]. Furthermore, a bank must maintain a robust grievance redressal mechanism that is not compromised by outsourcing, meaning the bank remains responsible for customer grievance redressal related to outsourced services [S3].

A commercial bank's agreement must include the bank's right to conduct audits on the service provider, whether by internal or external auditors, or by appointed agents, and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings [S2]. Furthermore, a bank's right to conduct regular audits of service providers, including subcontractors, can be done by the bank's internal or external auditors appointed on the bank's behalf [S3].

Yes, a commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided the arrangement is backed by a Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs/agreements with its group entities are in place [S1].

Yes, more than one RE, including a commercial bank, may adopt pooled (shared) audit when availing IT services from the same third-party service provider [S1]. This allows the relevant REs to either pool their audit resources or engage an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit the common service provider [S1]. However, the REs remain responsible for ensuring their respective contract audit requirements are met effectively [S1].

Additional considerations for outsourcing IT services include technology, infrastructural stability, data backup arrangements, and disaster recovery plan, as well as conflict of interest, capability to identify and segregate bank's data, and information/cyber security risk assessment [S1]. A bank must also evaluate the need for outsourcing based on materiality/criticality of the service, expectations, success factors, and cost-benefit analysis [S2].

A bank shall create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains [S2]. Furthermore, the bank must map its dependency on third parties and periodically evaluate the information received from the service providers [S2].

A commercial bank shall consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the associated costs, time, and resources [S1]. Additionally, a bank must require its service provider to develop and establish a robust framework for documenting, maintaining, and testing business continuity and recovery procedures [S3].

The Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated shall be responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Additionally, the Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated shall be responsible for approving a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S5].

Yes, the provisions apply to subcontracted activities [S3]. The outsourcing contract must provide for the prior approval or consent of the bank before a service provider engages any subcontractor for all or part of the outsourced activity [S3]. Before granting consent, the bank must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with the Directions set out in Chapter III [S3].

Commercial banks are prohibited from outsourcing core management functions, which include Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and management of investment portfolio [S2].

A bank must put in place a risk management framework that comprehensively deals with the processes and responsibilities for identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Furthermore, a bank shall have in place a management structure to monitor and control its outsourced activities, ensuring outsourcing agreements address this [S4]. The IT Function's responsibilities include assisting Senior Management in identifying, measuring, monitoring, mitigating, and managing the level of IT outsourcing risk [S2].

The Directions are titled the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 [S2]. The Directions are issued in exercise of powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 [S1].

Card-issuers must ensure that their call centre staff are trained adequately to competently handle and escalate a complaint if necessary [S1]. This requirement is also stated for Non-Banking Financial Companies [S2].

The co-branded card must explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a cobranding arrangement [S1]. Additionally, the co-branded card shall explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a cobranding arrangement [S5].

Card-issuers and their agents must adhere to the extant instructions on Fair Practices Code for lenders when recovering dues [S2]. Furthermore, agents must refrain from actions that could damage the card-issuer's integrity and reputation and observe strict customer confidentiality [S1].

Prior approval of the Reserve Bank is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards, and co-branded credit cards, subject to conditions stipulated under the relevant chapter [S1]. Furthermore, banks do not require prior approval to become a co-branding partner of card-issuers [S2].

If no consent is received for activating a credit card, card-issuers shall close the credit card account without any cost to the customer within seven working days from date of seeking confirmation from the customer [S2].

The monetary threshold is one percent of the credit limit or ₹5000, whichever is lower [S1]. This requirement applies to adjusting a credit amount beyond this cut-off arising from refund/failed/reversed transactions against the credit limit for which payment has already been made by the cardholder [S1].

The card-issuer must explicitly bring to the notice of the customer that the information relating to credit history or repayment record is being provided in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 [S1]. This requirement also applies to Non-Banking Financial Companies [S2].
All communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number, and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact [S2].

A bank shall report a credit card account as ‘past due’ to credit information companies (CICs) or levy penal charges only when a credit card account remains overdue for more than three days [S2]. Similarly, card-issuers shall report a credit card account as 'past due' or levy penal charges only when the account remains 'past due' for more than three days [S1].

Card-issuers shall not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholders at the time of issue of the card and without getting their explicit consent [S1]. This rule applies to Commercial Banks regarding Credit Cards and Debit Cards [S1]. However, this exclusion does not apply to charges like service taxes levied by the Government or any other statutory authority [S1].

Yes, card-issuers, which includes commercial banks, may issue business credit cards to business entities or individuals for business expenses [S1]. Business credit cards are issued to individuals for the purpose of business expenses with specified terms and conditions and not for personal use [S4].

A card-issuer must have a well-documented policy for credit card issuance and conduct, approved by its Board or a delegated Committee, and this policy must align with Reserve Bank instructions and these Directions, and be available on the card-issuer's website [S1]. This policy should cover aspects such as interest rate ceiling, default reporting to a CIC, co-branding, procedures for blocking, time for lost card formalities, and grievance redressal [S3]. Furthermore, terms must require the cardholder to keep the card safe and not record the PIN or code in an accessible form [S2].
Card-issuers must ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders [S1]. This requirement also applies to Non-Banking Financial Companies [S3].

Card-issuers must provide the cardholder a term-sheet containing the MITC, which should detail fees and charges, drawal limits, billing information, and procedures for default and circumstances [S4]. Additionally, the cardholder must be provided with a record of transactions immediately after completion, such as a receipt, bank statement, email, or SMS [S1]. The card-issuers must also provide the detailed procedure to report loss, theft, or unauthorized use via multiple 24x7 channels, which must be publicized in billing statements [S5].

The disclosure of customers’ information to DSAs, DMAs, or recovery agents shall be limited to the extent that will enable them to discharge their duties [S1]. Personal information provided by the cardholder but not required for recovery purposes shall not be released by the card-issuer [S1].

A bank shall have the freedom to determine interest on deposits of money accepted or renewed under the RFC Account Scheme, according to a comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated committee [S1]. Additionally, interest rates on NRE/NRO deposits cannot be higher than those offered on comparable domestic rupee term deposits [S2].

Interest shall be paid at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank and not at the contracted rate if the term deposit is withdrawn before the maturity date [S1]. However, no interest shall be paid if the premature withdrawal occurs before the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1) [S1].
The minimum tenor for NRE term deposits shall be one year, and for NRO term deposits, the minimum tenor shall be seven days [S1].
Rupee deposits of non-residents under NRE and NRO must only be accepted by banks authorized under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time [S1].

A bank may allow an additional interest of one per cent per annum over and above the rate mentioned in the schedule of interest rates on savings or term deposits for its staff and their exclusive associations, subject to certain conditions [S1]. This additional interest is payable until the person remains eligible or until the maturity of a term deposit account if eligibility ceases [S1].

If the claimant(s) of an NRE term deposit account of a deceased depositor are residents, the deposit on maturity shall be treated as a domestic rupee term deposit and interest shall be paid for the subsequent period at a rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity [S1].

The rate of interest on matured deposits for a deceased individual depositor or two or more joint depositors where one has died shall be as per the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits and subject to the conditions in paragraph 7 of these Directions [S2].

If the components of the penalty for premature withdrawal of FCNR(B) term deposits are not clearly brought to the notice of the depositors at the time of acceptance, the exchange loss arising out of premature withdrawal shall be borne by the bank [S1].

If the period from the date of maturity till the date of renewal does not exceed 14 days, the interest rate payable on the renewed FCNR(B) deposit shall be the appropriate rate prevailing on the date of maturity or on the date the depositor seeks renewal, whichever is lower [S1].

Any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S1]. All approvals or acknowledgments granted under these repealed lists shall be deemed as governed by these Directions [S1].

No penalty for premature withdrawal of a term deposit shall be levied if the amount of a term deposit is split at the request from the claimant(s) of deceased depositors or joint account holders, provided the period and aggregate amount of the deposit do not change [S2]. Additionally, no penalty for premature withdrawal shall be levied if depositors of a specific branch desire premature withdrawal consequent to the transfer of business to another bank [S4].

Yes, a bank may give its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates admissible to senior citizens over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of being retired members of the bank’s staff [S1].

The interest on the minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer is paid for the period from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month [S1]. This is subject to the conditions given in paragraph 7 of these Directions [S1].

A comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated Committee must cover the interest rate on deposits and penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits, including partial premature withdrawal [S2]. Furthermore, this policy must address penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits and FCNR(B) term deposits [S4].

A bank shall pay interest when converting an FCNR(B) Account into an RFC / Resident Rupee Account even if the minimum maturity period has not been completed, subject to conditions in paragraph 7 [S1]. The rate of interest shall not exceed the rate payable on savings bank deposits held under RFC Account Scheme [S1].

A commercial bank may use foreign currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB dated December 17, 2018, or foreign currency funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market for granting PCFC [S3].

A bank must satisfy itself that the direct remittance from abroad is against an export order, is as per trade practices, and is an approved method of realization of export proceeds when granting export credit to exporters with a good track record [S1]. For the 'Running Account' facility under the PCFC Scheme, the bank shall extend it only to exporters whose track record has been good [S3]. Furthermore, in cases where the 'Running Account' facility is extended, LCs or firm orders must be produced within a reasonable period of time [S3].

The exposure of a bank by way of PCEs to bonds issued by each such NBFC / HFC shall be restricted to one per cent of capital funds of the RE within the extant single / group borrower exposure limits [S1]. Additionally, the PCE exposure by the bank to a single counterparty or group of counterparties shall be within the overall regulatory exposure limits applicable to the bank [S5].

All corporates and other constituent borrowers with a turnover above a threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors must disclose the ‘aging schedule’ of their overdue payables in their periodical returns submitted to banks [S1].

A bank shall grant export credit to exporters with a good track record until the realization of proceeds from a cheque or draft received from abroad, provided it is against an export order, aligns with trade practices, and is an approved method of realization of export proceeds as per extant rules [S1].

The bank must take into account the customer suitability and appropriateness when introducing any kind of product [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure that borrowers/customers are fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products [S1].

The bank shall verify loan applications within a reasonable period of time and must intimate the borrower immediately if additional details or documents are required [S2]. Furthermore, market reports on builders/developers should be obtained, and loans should only be sanctioned for projects by reputed builders/developers [S1].

The builder/developer/company shall disclose in the Pamphlets/Brochures etc., the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged [S1]. Additionally, they must indicate in their pamphlets/brochures that they will provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC)/permission of the mortgagee bank for the sale of flats/property, if required [S1].

A commercial bank shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies or other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing [S1]. Furthermore, a bank shall not enter into a leasing agreement with another equipment leasing company and other non-banking finance company engaged in equipment leasing [S2].

Bills rediscounted 'with recourse' in the domestic market should only be reflected in the case of the first bank discounting the bills, as that bank alone has recourse to the exporter [S1]. The bank rediscounting shall not reckon the amount as export credit [S1].

The value of gold or silver accepted as collateral shall be based on the reference price corresponding to its actual purity [S2]. This reference price is the lower of the average closing price over the preceding 30 days or the closing price on the preceding day, as published by IBJA or a SEBI-regulated commodity exchange [S2].

All collateral-free loans provided to low-income households, defined as those with an annual income up to ₹3,00,000, are considered microfinance loans [S5]. For a microfinance loan to be collateral-free, it must not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by the hypothecation of any security [S5]. The definition of a microfinance loan is also referenced in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 [S4].

A commercial bank must capture and maintain project specific data in an electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis [S1]. The project finance database must include parameters such as Debtor Profile, Original Project Profile, and Change in DCCO [S1].

The bank shall not grant finance for the construction of buildings meant purely for Government / Semi-Government offices, including Municipal and Panchayat offices [S1]. However, the bank may grant loans for activities that will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD [S1].

A bank shall accept DLG in one or more of the following forms: cash deposited with the bank, a Fixed Deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, or a Bank Guarantee in favour of the bank [S1].

An Internet Banking Channel is a digital banking channel offered by a bank for operating accounts and accessing services over the internet, including web browser-based applications but excluding mobile applications [S1]. A Mobile Banking Channel is a digital banking channel offered by a bank for operating accounts and accessing services using mobile applications, USSD, and SMS [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may grant an extension of time or exempt a regulated entity from all or any provisions of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, if it considers it necessary for avoiding hardship or for any other just and sufficient reason [S1]. This exemption can be general or for a specified period, subject to conditions imposed by the Reserve Bank [S1].

Commercial banks must adhere to the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements, along with instructions on FEMA 1999 and relevant DPSS instructions [S1]. The jurisdiction for legal settlement within digital banking operations is within India [S1].

Banks must require prior approval of the Reserve Bank for launching a transactional banking facility, subject to fulfilling eligibility criteria such as implementing CBS and public facing IT infrastructure enabling IPv6 traffic, compliance with minimum regulatory CRAR, and meeting minimum paid up capital/Net worth [S1]. The application should be made to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India through the PRAVAAH portal [S1].

Yes, banks shall obtain explicit consent from the customer for registering or de-registering for digital banking services, and this consent must be duly recorded/documented [S1]. Furthermore, it must be clearly indicated that SMS/email alerts will be sent to the customer's registered mobile number/email for both financial and non-financial operations [S1].

The interpretation of any provision of the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions by the RBI shall be final and binding [S1]. Similarly, the interpretation of any provision of these Directions by RBI shall be final and binding on all concerned entities [S4].

A commercial bank must comply with the Guidelines on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services specified in Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, as amended from time to time [S1]. Furthermore, the outsourced model for the digital banking segment must specifically comply with the relevant regulatory guidelines on outsourcing contained in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 [S2].

To provide a view only banking facility, a bank must have implemented a Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled its public facing Information technology (IT) infrastructure to handle Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) traffic [S1]. The bank must also intimate the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India, through the PRAVAAH portal, along with a 'Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy' (GAICA) report within thirty days of the decision to launch the facility [S1].

Banks must put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels, taking into account all statutory and regulatory requirements, including those concerning the management of liquidity and operational risks in a digital banking scenario [S1].

All banks offering digital banking services must comply with the Directions contained in Chapter IV on a continuous basis [S2]. Furthermore, instructions applicable to digital banking services include guidelines from the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 [S2].

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025 apply to banks offering digital banking services [S1]. All banks offering digital banking services, regardless of the type of facility, must comply with the Directions in Chapter IV on a continuous basis [S1].

The bank shall consider lodging a formal complaint against the statutory auditors with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) / Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) [S1]. Pending disciplinary action, the complaints shall be forwarded to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and Indian Banks' Association (IBA) [S1]. Before reporting, the bank must satisfy itself of the auditors' involvement and provide them an opportunity to be heard [S1].

The responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank [S1]. Furthermore, a bank furnishing information to credit information companies must ensure the accuracy of the particulars of the directors, preferably by cross-checking with the Registrar of Companies database [S1].

The bar on additional credit facility to a wilful defaulter or any associated entity shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of the wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders [S1].

The name of a borrower or guarantor classified as a wilful defaulter shall be removed from the LWD after the implementation of the resolution plan under IBC or the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025, if the account was in LWD and subsequently underwent liquidation or the resolution resulted in a change in the management and control of the entity/business enterprise [S2].

A commercial bank shall put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identification of wilful defaulters so that the penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated [S1].

A bank must submit information in Annex II to all credit information companies at monthly intervals regarding wilful defaulters, including a list of wilful defaulters (LWD) for suit filed accounts and a LWD for non-suit filed accounts [S1]. Additionally, a bank must promptly inform credit information companies of the removal of a wilful defaulter's name from the LWD if the outstanding amount falls below ₹25 lakh or as notified by the Reserve Bank of India [S1].

Before transferring a defaulted loan with an outstanding of ₹25 lakh and above, a commercial bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective [S1]. This process need not necessarily involve a two-stage committee but must ensure a thorough examination of wilful default aspects for each defaulted loan [S1].

A commercial bank should forward the details of these third parties to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, regardless of the bank's membership status with the IBA [S1]. Before reporting to IBA, the bank must satisfy itself of the concerned third parties' involvement and provide them an opportunity to be heard, following a suitably recorded due process [S1].

Yes, when a default occurs in making payment or repayment by the principal debtor, a bank can proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor [S1]. Furthermore, the liability of the guarantor is immediate when a bank has made a claim on the guarantor due to the principal debtor's default [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may issue necessary clarifications to give effect to the provisions of the Directions or remove difficulties in their application or interpretation [S2]. The interpretation of any provision of these Directions given by the Reserve Bank shall be final and binding [S2].

A commercial bank shall report to credit information companies the details of guarantors who have failed to honour the commitments when invoked, as large defaulters or wilful defaulters, as the case may be [S1]. The details must be reported as per Annex I and II [S1].

These Directions are applicable to commercial banks, which include all banking companies, corresponding new banks, and State Bank of India as defined under section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 [S4]. However, they exclude Small Finance Banks (SFBs), Local Area Banks (LABs), Payments Banks (PBs), and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) [S4].
A bank shall require its internal auditors to specifically look into adherence to instructions for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter [S1].

The contents of the Master Direction must be read along with other relevant governing statutes [S1].

A proposal for the appointment of a new MD&CEO/CEO must be submitted to the RBI at least four months before the expiry of the term of office of the present incumbent [S1].

The change in tenor premium should not be borrower specific or loan class specific, meaning the tenor premium will be uniform for all types of loans for a given residual tenor [S1]. A bank's Board-approved policy delineating the components of spread charged to a customer must include principles to determine the quantum of each component, the range of spread for a given category of borrower/type of loan, and to delegate powers in respect of loan pricing [S1].

A bank can calculate the cost of funds on the basis of average cost of funds, marginal cost of funds, or any other reasonable and transparent methodology [S3]. This chosen methodology must be consistent and made available for supervisory review or scrutiny when required [S3].

Yes, the credit risk premium charged to an existing borrower may be increased due to deterioration in the credit risk profile of the customer [S1]. Negative carry on the mandatory CRR, when returns on CRR balances are nil, will be calculated as: Required CRR x (marginal cost) / (1- CRR) [S1]. The marginal cost of funds used for this calculation shall be the one arrived at in paragraph 17 [S1].

The NBFC shall register the details of a non-profit organisation customer on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog if they are not registered [S1]. If an NBFC suspects money laundering or terrorist financing and reasonably believes that performing the CDD process will tip off the customer, it shall not pursue the CDD process and instead file an STR with FIU-IND [S1].

The NBFC shall verify the ‘UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List of Designated Individuals and Entities‘ every day [S1]. This verification must account for any modifications such as additions, deletions, or other changes [S1].

Yes, the NBFC shall have the option to hold 'pooled' accounts managed by professional intermediaries on behalf of entities like mutual funds or pension funds [S1].

These loans should not be included in the numerator (microfinance loans) or the denominator (total assets) when determining compliance with the minimum threshold of microfinance loans [S1].

An NBFC-MFI must adhere to the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 regarding the treatment of deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities for capital computation [S1].

An NBFC-MFI must maintain a capital adequacy ratio of not less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk weighted assets of on-balance sheet and of risk adjusted value of off-balance sheet items [S2]. For calculating exposure amount, an NBFC measures off-balance exposure differently for credit protections, non-eligible credit risk mitigants, and derivatives contracts [S3]. The aggregate of risk-adjusted value of on-balance sheet assets is taken into account for reckoning the minimum capital ratio [S1].

An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 [S5]. Additionally, the NBFC-MFI must comply with the registration requirements specified under Chapter III of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025 [S2].
An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025 [S5].

All other provisions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025, shall be applicable to NBFC-MFIs unless they are contradictory to the contents of the NBFC-MFI directions [S3].

An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Additionally, an NBFC-MFI must adhere to paragraphs 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 regarding opening a branch/representative office abroad and closure of branches [S3]. An NBFC must obtain prior approval of the RBI for opening a subsidiary/joint venture or undertaking investment abroad [S4].
An NBFC that does not qualify as an NBFC-MFI may extend microfinance loans that in aggregate do not exceed 25 per cent of its total assets [S2].

Standard assets are one of the classes into which an NBFC shall classify its lease/hire purchase assets, loans and advances, and any other forms of credit, after considering credit weaknesses and dependence on collateral security [S2]. The standard assets provisioning for microfinance loans of an NBFC-MFI in a particular layer of the scale-based regulatory framework must follow the instructions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 for that layer [S1].

An NBFC-MFI shall maintain a capital adequacy ratio consisting of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital which shall not be less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk weighted assets of on-balance sheet and of risk adjusted value of off-balance sheet items [S1].

An NBFC-MFI shall ensure adherence to several specific directions, including those on Responsible Business Conduct, Know Your Customer, Securitisation Transactions, Credit Information Reporting, Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters, and Chapter II and III of Miscellaneous Directions [S1]. Furthermore, the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025 shall be applicable to NBFC-MFI registered with the RBI under the provisions of the RBI Act, 1934 [S2]. An NBFC-MFI must also adhere to directions on credit facilities and various financial services, such as the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 [S5].

Any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S1]. Specifically for NBFC-MFI, the repeal of existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines is communicated vide circular DOR.RRC.REC.302/33-01-010/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025 [S5].
The passages do not specify a deadline for an NBFC lender's quarterly regulatory statements to reach the relevant RBI Regional Office. [S2]
An NBFC-P2P shall comply with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices dated November 07, 2023 (as amended from time to time) [S1].

An NBFC shall have Board approved policies and review mechanisms in place to ensure responsible business conduct, which includes a Fair Practices Code and a grievance redressal mechanism [S1]. The Board of Directors must also provide for the periodical review of the compliance of the Fair Practices Code and the functioning of the grievance redressal mechanism at various levels of management, with a consolidated report submitted to the Board regularly [S4].

An NBFC-P2P must maintain at least two escrow accounts: one for funds received from lenders and pending disbursal (Lenders’ escrow Account), and another for collections from borrowers (Borrowers’ escrow Account) [S1]. Funds from the lenders’ bank accounts go to the Lenders’ Escrow Account, and repayments from the borrower's bank account go to the Borrowers’ Escrow Account [S1].

An NBFC-P2P requires prior written permission from the Reserve Bank for any allotment of shares that will bring the aggregate holding of an individual or group to the equivalent of 26 per cent and more of the paid-up capital of the NBFC-P2P [S1].

An Information System Audit of the internal systems and processes for an NBFC-P2P shall be conducted at least once in two years by CISA certified external auditors [S1]. The report must be submitted to the Regional Office of the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank, under whose jurisdiction the Registered Office of the NBFC-P2P is located, within one month of submission by the external auditor [S1].
An NBFC-P2P may make use of the ‘Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience’, as amended from time to time [S1].

Yes, the provisions in several directions shall be applicable to an NBFC-P2P, where not contradictory to the contents of these Directions [S1]. These applicable directions include those on Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation, Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends, Credit Information Reporting, Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures, Governance, Acquisition of Shareholding or Control, Managing Risks in Outsourcing, and Responsible Business Conduct [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may specify any other condition necessary to ensure that commencing or carrying on the business in India will not be prejudicial to the public interest [S2]. Additionally, the Reserve Bank may impose any other condition it deems fit when granting in-principle approval [S3] or a Certificate of Registration (CoR) [S5].

An NBFC-P2P must comply with the relevant instructions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025, for reporting and updating credit information related to borrower transactions on the platform [S1]. For this purpose, the NBFC-P2P must include necessary consents in the agreement with participants for providing the credit information [S1].
For an NBFC-P2P, the Leverage Ratio is defined as the Total Outside Liabilities divided by Owned Funds [S4]. An NBFC-P2P shall maintain a Leverage Ratio not exceeding two [S1].

No, an NBFC-P2P shall not hold on its own balance sheet, funds received from lenders for lending, or funds received from borrowers for servicing loans [S1]. Customers’ funds lent/borrowed by using the platform is not reckoned as outside liability of the platform [S2].

The provisions in the directions mentioned shall be applicable to an NBFC-P2P where they are not contradictory to the contents of these Directions [S1]. An NBFC-P2P must remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025 [S3].

An NBFC-P2P must communicate changes of address, directors, and auditors as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Additionally, an NBFC-P2P must advise the Reserve Bank of any change of Directors or key management personnel [S4].

An NBFC-P2P must comply with the provisions of paragraphs 8 to 10 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025 [S5]. Additionally, it shall ensure compliance with the instructions prescribed in paragraphs 11 to 13 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Furthermore, compliance with paragraphs 6(1) and 6(2) of the same Directions is required [S3].

An NBFC-P2P shall put in place a Fair Practices Code, based on the Guidelines outlined herein, with the approval of its Board [S1]. The Fair Practices Code is one of the policies that the NBFC-P2P shall put in place and establish periodic review mechanisms for, and it must be approved by the Board or its Committee(s) [S4].
An NBFC-AA shall form a Nomination Committee consisting of not less than three members of its Board of Directors [S1].

NBFC-AA shall comply with the disclosure requirements in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025, except for provisions in paragraphs 13 to 15 and paragraph 20 [S3]. These Directions, excluding paragraphs 13 to 15 and 20, are applicable to NBFC-AA registered with the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 [S5]. The specified disclosures are in addition to and not in substitution of requirements under other laws, regulations, or accounting standards [S3].

An NBFC-AA shall communicate changes regarding address, directors, and auditors as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 [S1].

The Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 apply to every non-banking financial company undertaking the business of Account Aggregator as defined therein [S1]. The NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) consolidates financial information held by a customer with different financial entities [S2].

An NBFC-AA is defined as an 'Account Aggregator' as per Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Specific directions apply to NBFC-AA registered with the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934, such as those on Financial Statements [S4] and Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends [S3]. An NBFC-AA shall perform the function of obtaining, submitting, and managing customer consent in accordance with its directions [S5].

The interpretation of any provision of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 shall be final and binding, as stated in the context of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 [S1].

Financial information provided by a Financial Information Provider to an NBFC-AA for transfer to a Financial Information User shall not be used or disclosed by the NBFC-AA or the Financial Information User except as specified in the consent artefact [S1]. This applies when the information was provided with the customer's explicit consent [S2].

The NBFC-AA must verify the identity of the Financial Information User before securely transferring the customer’s information to the intended recipient, provided the information was provided with the customer's explicit consent [S1]. The transfer must be in accordance with the terms of the consent artefact [S1]. Furthermore, the information shall not be used or disclosed by the NBFC-AA or the Financial Information User except as specified in the consent artefact [S2].

An NBFC-AA would require a Board approved policy for pricing of services [S1]. This pricing must conform strictly with the internal guidelines adopted by the NBFC-AA, which need to be transparent and available in the public domain [S1]. Additionally, the NBFC-AA shall put in place Board approved policies for Pricing of Services [S4].

NBFC-AA shall always remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure specified in Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Specifically, NBFC-AA will always remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure [S2].
The NBFC-AA must ensure its IT systems have all necessary features to carry out its functions strictly in conformity with the Directions as updated from time to time [S5].

A standardized consent artefact obtained by the NBFC-AA must include the customer's identity and optional contact information, the nature and purpose of the financial information requested, the identity of recipients, a notification URL, consent creation and expiry dates, and the NBFC-AA's identity and signature [S1]. The NBFC-AA must inform the customer of all necessary attributes for the consent artefact and the right to file complaints [S2].

An NBFC-AA shall not undertake any other business other than the business of account aggregator [S4]. Furthermore, an NBFC-AA shall not use or access any customer information other than for performing the business of account aggregator explicitly requested by the customer [S1]. Financial information provided to an NBFC-AA shall not be used or disclosed except as may be specified in the consent artefact [S2].

Yes, a company seeking registration as an NBFC-AA with less than ₹2 crore in Net Owned Fund can meet the criteria within the period of validity of the in-principle approval for grant of certification of registration given by the Reserve Bank [S1].

A CI, which includes an NBFC, shall include in its loan policies/credit appraisal processes suitable provisions for obtaining CIRs from one or more CICs so that credit decisions are based on credit information available in the system [S2].

The reporting of Relationship Segment (RS) data by a CI to CICs is mandatory for all accounts opened on or after July 01, 2018 [S2].

A CI covered under the Internal Ombudsman framework shall adhere to the instructions issued vide Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2023 dated December 29, 2023 (as amended from time to time) [S3]. Additionally, a CI covered under the Internal Ombudsman framework shall adhere to the instructions issued vide Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2023 dated December 29, 2023 (as amended from time to time) [S4].
The convenor must send the meeting agenda and notes at least fifteen (15) days before the scheduled meeting [S2].

The Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025, do not state that they override other applicable laws; rather, one passage mentions that the application of other laws not barred is covered under Chapter-VII, Section B [S1]. Furthermore, in the context of NBFC-P2P, the provisions of the Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025, are applicable where not contradictory to the contents of other specified Directions [S2].
The Technical Working Group shall review the data reporting formats at least once a year [S2]. If any recommendations are made, they shall be made to the Reserve Bank [S2].

The Standing Sub-Group of TWG functions as an advisory and collaborative body to offer expert insights and make recommendations on technical aspects of credit information reporting [S2]. Its purpose is to support in-depth discussions regarding challenges encountered by CIs and CICs in relation to credit information reporting [S2]. This includes supporting necessary modifications, such as changes in IT systems, required in data reporting formats [S2].

A Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (RBIOS, 2021) shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S2]. Additionally, a CI covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S1].
The Sub-Group of TWG for Non-Banking Financial Companies shall meet at least on a half yearly basis to discuss credit information reporting issues and seek potential resolutions [S2].

The TWG comprises representatives from Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), All India Notified Financial Institutions (AIFIs), Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), India Banks’ Association (IBA), Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN), Sa-Dhan, and CICs [S2].

PAN or equivalent e-document of customers must be obtained and verified while undertaking transactions as per the provisions of Income Tax Rule 114B applicable to ARCs [S2]. Form 60 must be obtained from persons who do not have a PAN or equivalent e-document thereof [S2].

No, if an existing KYC-compliant customer of an ARC desires to open another account or avail of any other product or service from the same ARC, there shall be no need for a fresh CDD exercise as far as identification of the customer is concerned [S1].

The ARC shall register the details of a non-profit organisation customer on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog if they are not registered [S1]. The ARC must also maintain such registration records for five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later [S1].

The ARC shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks [S1]. The ARC shall carry out ‘Money Laundering (ML) and Terrorist Financing (TF) Risk Assessment’ exercises periodically to identify, assess and take effective measures to mitigate its money laundering and terrorist financing risk [S2]. Furthermore, the ARC shall adopt a risk-based approach to manage and mitigate ML/TF risks when developing new products and practices [S3].

The ARC shall review its risk assessment at least annually [S1]. The Board or a committee of the Board to which the power has been delegated shall determine the periodicity of the risk assessment exercise, in alignment with the outcome of the risk assessment exercise [S1].
The NBFC shall undertake diligence measures and meticulous monitoring to identify accounts which are operated as Money Mules and take appropriate action [S1].

KYC verification done by one branch or office of the NBFC is valid for transferring the account to any other branch or office of the same NBFC, provided the NBFC has completed full KYC verification and it is not due for periodic updation [S1].

A delay of each day in not reporting a transaction or delay of each day in rectifying a mis-represented transaction beyond the time limit as specified in the Rule shall constitute as a separate violation for an NBFC when furnishing information to the Director, FIU-IND [S1].

Yes, the directions apply to the branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of an All India Financial Institution located abroad, to the extent they are not contradictory to the local laws in the host country [S1]. If there is a variance in KYC/AML standards between the RBI and host country regulators, the branches/subsidiaries must adopt the more stringent regulation [S1].

The AIFI shall undertake identification of customers when carrying out any international money transfer operations for a person who is not an account holder of the AIFI [S1]. This requirement is also covered under the ordering AIFI ensuring required and accurate originator and beneficiary information for cross-border wire transfers [S2].
For opening an account of a trust, the bank must obtain the registration certificate, the trust deed, and the PAN or Form No.60 of the trust [S1].

The four key elements that an All India Financial Institution's KYC policy must include are Customer Acceptance Policy, Risk Management, Customer Identification Procedures (CIP), and Monitoring of Transactions [S1].
An AIFI shall capture customer’s KYC records and upload onto CKYCR within 10 days of commencement of an account-based relationship with the customer [S1].

A rural co-operative bank shall have a risk-based approach for risk management [S1]. The bank shall adopt a risk-based approach for periodic updation of KYC [S2]. Furthermore, the bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks and have Board-approved policies, controls and procedures in this regard [S5].

The 'at par' cheque facility for a rural co-operative bank shall only be utilized for their own use, for KYC compliant account-holders with transactions of ₹50,000 or more strictly by debit to customer accounts, or for walk-in customers against cash for less than ₹50,000 per individual [S2]. [S2]

An Urban Co-operative Bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks [S1]. The bank must have Board-approved policies, controls, and procedures in this regard [S1].
All transactions of ₹50,000 or more for KYC compliant account holders must be strictly by debit to the customers’ accounts [S1]. This requirement is also stated for Rural Co-operative Banks [S2].

A Regional Rural Bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for the mitigation and management of risks [S2]. This approach must also include categorizing customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on the bank's assessment and risk perception [S1]. The risk categorization should be based on parameters such as the customer’s identity, social/financial status, nature of business activity, and transaction details [S1].

The aggregate balance of all the deposit accounts of the customer shall not exceed Rupees One Lakh [S1]. If the balance exceeds this threshold, the bank shall cease the account’s operation until it completes the CDD as mentioned at (5) below [S1].

The bank, its directors, officers, and all employees of a Payments Bank must ensure that the fact of maintenance of records referred to in rule 3 of the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and furnishing of the information to the Director is confidential [S3]. However, this confidentiality requirement does not prevent sharing information under paragraph 8 of these Directions regarding any analysis of unusual transactions and activities, if such an analysis was performed [S3].
A delay of each day in not reporting a transaction to the Director, FIU-IND shall constitute as a separate violation [S1].

No, a Payments Bank shall not require Customer Due Diligence (CDD) of all the members of a Self Help Group (SHG) while opening the savings bank account of the SHG [S1]. The CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].

A small finance bank must put in place an adequate screening mechanism, including a Know Your Employee / Staff policy, as an integral part of its personnel recruitment/hiring process [S1]. The bank must also endeavor to ensure that staff dealing with/being deployed for KYC/AML/CFT matters have high integrity and ethical standards, a good understanding of extant KYC/AML/CFT standards, effective communication skills, and the ability to keep up with the changing KYC/AML/CFT landscape nationally and internationally [S1].
